questions.question: Choose the word that is the most appropriate synonym of the word "grin".
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **smile**.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **'grin'** refers to a **broad smile**, often one that shows the **teeth**, indicating high spirits, **amusement**, or satisfaction. (दाँत निकालकर मुस्कुराना)
 
 
• **Example: **He gave a sheepish **grin** when he was caught playing a prank.
 
 
 
• **'Smile'** is a **facial expression** characterized by the upward curving of the corners of the mouth, typically used to express **happiness**, **pleasure**, or **approval**. (मुस्कान)
 
 
• **Example: **She had a kind **smile** that put everyone at ease.
 
 
 
• Hence, we can infer that the most appropriate **synonym** of **'grin'** is **'smile'**.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **smile**.

**Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

__
 
• **Cry** (रोना): To shed **tears** as an expression of **distress**, pain, or sorrow.
 
 
• **Example: **The child began to **cry** when he fell down in the park.
 
 
 
• **Shout** (चिल्लाना): To speak or call out **suddenly** and **loudly**, often to express strong **emotion** or to be heard at a distance.
 
 
• **Example: **He had to **shout** to get the attention of the lifeguard.
 
 
 
• **Yawn** (जम्हाई लेना): An **involuntary** act of opening the mouth wide and inhaling deeply, usually due to **tiredness** or **boredom**.
 
 
• **Example: **I couldn't help but **yawn** during the long and tedious meeting.

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?
She had sold the house years before the real estate boom.

options.text: The house has been sold by her years before the real estate boom.
The house was sold by her years before the real estate boom.
The house had been sold by her years before the real estate boom.
The house had sold by her years before the real estate boom.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The house had been sold by her years before the real estate boom.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The given sentence is in the **Active Voice** and uses the **Past Perfect Tense**. The structure of the sentence is: **Subject (She)** + **had** + **V3 (sold)** + **Object (the house)** + **Adverbial Phrase (years before the real estate boom)**.

• To transform a sentence from **Active Voice** to **Passive Voice** in the **Past Perfect Tense**, the following structural formula is applied: **New Subject (Object of Active)** + **had** + **been** + **V3 (Past Participle)** + **by** + **New Object (Subject of Active)**.

• The **Object** of the active sentence, **the house**, shifts to the **Subject** position in the passive sentence.

• The auxiliary verb **had been** must be used to maintain the **Past Perfect** aspect while indicating the **Passive Voice**.

• The main verb **sold** remains in its **Past Participle (V3)** form, which is standard for all passive constructions.

• The **Subject** of the active sentence, **She**, is converted into its **Objective Case** pronoun, which is **her**, and is preceded by the preposition **by**.

• The prepositional phrase **years before the real estate boom** remains unchanged as it provides the temporal context for the action.

 **Additional Information__**

• Understanding the tense discrepancies in the incorrect options:

• **Present Perfect Passive**: Option 1 uses **has been sold**. This is the **Present Perfect** form, which indicates an action connected to the present, whereas the original sentence describes an action completed before another past event.

• **Simple Past Passive**: Option 2 uses **was sold**. While this is a past tense, it fails to capture the **Past Perfect** nuance (the past of the past) established by **had sold**.

• **Structural Incompleteness**: Option 4 uses **had sold** in a passive-looking structure but omits the word **been**. Without **been**, the sentence does not function as a passive construction and remains grammatically incorrect in this context.

• **Pronoun Transformation**: In English grammar, when the subject **She** (nominative) moves to the object position (after **by**), it must always change to **her** (accusative).

</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?
The annual science exhibitions are organised by the school authorities with great enthusiasm.

options.text: The school authorities organise the annual science exhibitions with great enthusiasm.
The annual science exhibitions have been organised by the school authorities with great enthusiasm.
The school authorities had organised the annual science exhibitions with great enthusiasm.
The school authorities will organise the annual science exhibitions with great enthusiasm.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The school authorities organise the annual science exhibitions with great enthusiasm.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The provided sentence is in the **Passive Voice** and follows the structure of the **Simple Present Tense**: **Object + is/am/are + V3 (Past Participle) + by + Agent**.

• In the passive sentence, **The annual science exhibitions** acts as the object receiving the action, and **the school authorities** is the agent performing the action.

• To convert the sentence into the **Active Voice**, the agent **the school authorities** must be shifted to the **Subject** position at the beginning of the sentence.

• The verb phrase **are organised** (passive form) is converted to the **Active Verb** form **organise**. Since the new subject **the school authorities** is **plural**, the verb follows the **Subject-Verb Agreement** rule for the simple present tense without the suffix -s or -es.

• The original subject **The annual science exhibitions** is moved to the **Object** position, appearing immediately after the main verb.

• The prepositional phrase **with great enthusiasm** remains at the end as an **Adverbial Modifier** to retain the original context and manner of the action.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Active vs. Passive Voice Fundamentals**:

• **Active Voice**: The subject of the sentence performs the action. Structure: **Subject + Verb + Object**. It is generally more direct and concise.

• **Passive Voice**: The subject of the sentence is the recipient of the action. Structure: **Object + form of be + V3 + by + Agent**. It is used when the actor is unknown or less important than the action itself.

• **Tense Preservation in Voice Conversion**:

• **Simple Present**: Active (**V1/V1+s/es**) changes to Passive (**is/am/are + V3**).

• **Present Perfect**: Active (**has/have + V3**) changes to Passive (**has/have + been + V3**). Option 2 uses a form of this tense, which is incorrect here.

• **Past Perfect**: Active (**had + V3**) changes to Passive (**had + been + V3**). Option 3 uses this tense, which changes the timeline of the original sentence.

• **Simple Future**: Active (**will + V1**) changes to Passive (**will + be + V3**). Option 4 incorrectly shifts the meaning to the future.

</ul

questions.question:
In the given question, a sentence is divided into four parts and given in the alternatives (A), (B), (C), and (D). There is an error in one part. Choose the alternative containing that part of the sentence that has the error. Choosing the alternative with the error will be the answer.
Let's move all the books kept on this shelf on the upper one and make space for the new books purchased from the market today.

options.text: Let's move all the books kept on this
shelf on the upper one and
make space for the new books

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The primary error in the sentence lies in the use of the preposition **on** in part **B**.
 
• The verb **move** indicates a transition or change of location from one point to another, which typically requires the preposition **to** to indicate the destination.
 
• While **on** describes a static position atop something, **to** is used to show the direction of the movement.
 
• The correct phrase should be **to the upper one** instead of **on the upper one**.
 
• Thus, the error is located in **part B** of the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is **B**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *'Let's move all the books kept on this shelf **to the upper one** and make space for the new books purchased from the market today.'*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Part A: 'Let's move all the books kept on this'** – This part is grammatically correct as it correctly identifies the objects being acted upon.
 
• **Part C: 'make space for the new books'** – This part is correct; the phrase **make space for** is the standard idiomatic expression.
 
• **Part D: 'purchased from the market today.'** – This part is grammatically correct, using the past participle **purchased** to describe the books.

questions.question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

They are lacking ____ minimum courtesy.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**in**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **lacking** in this sentence functions as an **adjective** (or a present participle used as an adjective) meaning deficient in or not having enough of something.
 
• Standard English grammar requires the preposition **in** to follow the adjective **lacking** when specifying the quality or attribute that is missing.
 
• Common idiomatic expressions include being **lacking in confidence**, **lacking in resources**, or **lacking in courtesy**.
 
• **Options 1, 3, and 4** do not follow the standard idiomatic usage with the word **lacking** in this context.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Complete Sentence:** *'They are **lacking in**__ minimum courtesy.'*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• **Lack (Verb):** When **lack** is used as a verb, it is transitive and takes no preposition. Example: 'They **lack** basic manners.'
 
• **Lack (Noun):** When **lack** is used as a noun, it is usually followed by the preposition **of**. Example: 'There is a **lack of** courtesy in their behavior.'
 
• **Lacking (Adjective):** When **lacking** is used as an adjective (following a form of the verb 'to be'), the preposition **in** is the correct choice. Example: 'He is **lacking in** experience.'

questions.question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. Pure chance led my friend Hercule Poirot, formerly chief of the Belgian force, to be connected with the Styles Case. 

A. Having been wounded on the Somme and invalidated out of the Army, I finally took up my quarters with him in London. 

B. In doing so, I feel that I cannot do better than begin with that strange tangle which aroused such widespread public interest at the time. 

C. Since I have a firsthand knowledge of most of his cases, it has been suggested to me that I select some of the most interesting and place them on record. 

D. His success brought him notoriety, and he decided to devote himself to the solving of problems in crime. 

S2. I refer to the affair at the Victory Ball.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**__Key Points__**

 
• The paragraph begins by describing the origin of **Hercule Poirot**'s career as a private detective following a specific case. 
• **Sentence D is the first sentence** as it provides a direct consequence of the **Styles Case** mentioned in S1: 
• 'His success brought him notoriety, and he decided to devote himself to the solving of problems in crime.' 
• **Sentence A follows** as it introduces the narrator's personal background and explains how he came to reside with Poirot in **London**: 
• 'Having been wounded on the Somme and invalidated out of the Army, I finally took up my quarters with him in London.' 
• **Sentence C is the third sentence** because it builds on the narrator's proximity to Poirot, explaining that his **firsthand knowledge** led to the suggestion that he record the cases: 
• 'Since I have a firsthand knowledge of most of his cases, it has been suggested to me that I select some of the most interesting and place them on record.' 
• **Sentence B is the fourth** as the phrase 'In doing so' refers back to the act of recording cases mentioned in C, and it introduces a specific **strange tangle**: 
• 'In doing so, I feel that I cannot do better than begin with that strange tangle which aroused such widespread public interest at the time.' 
• The final fixed sentence S2 completes the thought by identifying the case as the affair at the **Victory Ball**. 
• The correct sequence is **DACB**. 

 

**Coherent paragraph after rearrangement**:

'Pure chance led my friend **Hercule Poirot**, formerly chief of the Belgian force, to be connected with the **Styles Case**. His success brought him **notoriety**, and he decided to devote himself to the solving of problems in crime. Having been wounded on the **Somme** and invalidated out of the **Army**, I finally took up my quarters with him in **London**. Since I have a **firsthand knowledge** of most of his cases, it has been suggested to me that I select some of the most interesting and place them on record. In doing so, I feel that I cannot do better than begin with that **strange tangle** which aroused such widespread public interest at the time. I refer to the affair at the **Victory Ball**.'</div

• **Sentence D follows S1** because it provides immediate detail about how Richard navigated the **wild and rough country** mentioned in the first sentence:

• **Sentence A follows D** as it provides the justification for his secrecy and fear of being recognized:
 
 
• 'For in those **rude times** no stranger was safe in a foreign land and a **shipwrecked king** would have been a fine prize.'

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. If you feel Options A, B, or C do not improve the sentence, then choose Option D: "No improvement required."

__The reason why I am confused is because__ they are giving me mixed signals.

options.text: Why am I confused is because
The reason for my confusion is because

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**I am confused because**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence contains a **redundant** expression, also known as a **pleonasm**. The phrase **the reason** and the **subordinating conjunction** **because** both indicate **causality**. Using them together in a single clause is considered **tautological** in standard English.
 
• The word **reason** acts as a noun that points to a cause, while **because** introduces the cause itself. Grammatically, 'the reason' should be followed by a **complement clause** starting with **that** (e.g., 'The reason is that...'), not an adverbial clause starting with 'because'.
 
• Option 3, **I am confused because**, provides the most **direct** and **concise** way to convey the message. It eliminates the **wordiness** of the original sentence by removing the unnecessary subject phrase 'The reason why'.
 
• In **Sentence Improvement** tasks, the goal is to choose the option that is both **grammatically accurate** and **stylistically superior**. Simplifying the structure to **Subject + Verb + Conjunction** ensures clarity and follows the **principle of economy** in language.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• Analysis of incorrect options:
 
 
• **Why am I confused is because**: This option incorrectly uses an **interrogative word order** ('Why am I') within a **declarative sentence**. Furthermore, it retains the **redundancy** between 'Why' and 'because'.
 
• **The reason for my confusion is because**: While it replaces 'why I am confused' with a **noun phrase**, it fails to correct the fundamental **grammatical error** of pairing 'reason' with 'because'. A correct alternative would have been 'The reason for my confusion is **that**'.
 
• **Redundancy Rule**: Common redundant phrases often tested include 'return back', 'reason why... because', 'repeat again', and 'sufficient enough'. Removing the repetitive element is a standard **error detection** strategy.
 
• **Conjunction usage**: **Because** is a **subordinating conjunction** that connects a dependent clause to an independent clause. When the purpose of the sentence is to state a fact directly, starting with the subject is preferred over complex **nominalizations**.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
Choose the option that correctly fills in the blank in the sentence below.

"Scientists who work on spaceship development often __________ with challenges that extend beyond terrestrial experiences."
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The subject of the sentence is **Scientists**, which is a **plural noun**.
 
• According to the rules of **subject-verb agreement**, a plural subject must be paired with the base form of the verb (plural verb) in the simple present tense.
 
• The word **often** acts as an adverb of frequency, suggesting that the sentence describes a general fact or habitual action, requiring the **simple present tense**.
 
• The term **graple** (a variant/misspelling of **grapple**) functions as the plural form of the verb, matching the subject **Scientists**.
 
• Therefore, **Option 3** is the grammatically appropriate choice to fill the blank.

Therefore, the correct answer is **graple**.

 

**Complete Passage:** *In the annals of human achievement, the development of the spaceship stands as a monumental testament to the ingenuity and perseverance of scientists. Unlike any other invention, spaceships have revolutionized our understanding of the cosmos, allowing us to venture beyond Earth's atmosphere and unlock the mysteries of the universe. These vehicles are not merely mechanical constructs but intricate systems composed of advanced technology, engineering precision, and sheer human determination. Spaceships require a **confluence** of various scientific disciplines. Aerospace engineers meticulously design the structure, ensuring the spacecraft can withstand the extreme conditions of space, including vacuum, radiation, and temperature fluctuations. Astrophysicists provide crucial insights into celestial bodies and cosmic phenomena, guiding mission trajectories and objectives. Meanwhile, biologists study how living organisms can survive and adapt to the hostile environment beyond our planet, which is crucial for manned missions. Scientists who work on spaceship development often **graple** with challenges that extend beyond terrestrial experiences. The absence of gravity **affects** both the mechanical operations of the spacecraft and the physiological well-being of astronauts. Communication delays, sometimes spanning min, complicate real-time decision-making. Despite these **formidable** obstacles, the collective efforts of multidisciplinary teams have repeatedly demonstrated triumph over adversity, pushing the very boundaries of human exploration. As humanity stands on the cusp of deeper interstellar journeys, the collaboration between centers of research, innovation, and space agencies worldwide is more vital than ever. These centers not only foster technological advancements but also cultivate the next generation of scientists who will carry the beacon of space exploration forward.*

 

**Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1 (grappled):** This is the **past tense** form. While grammatically sound in isolation, the passage context uses the present tense to describe ongoing scientific work.
 
• **Option 2 (grappling):** This is the **present participle** (-ing form). It cannot function as the main verb without an auxiliary verb (like 'are').
